query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of boron carbide to ZrB2 powders will enable in-situ formation of a transient eutectic liquid during sintering at reduced temperatures (~1700–2000 °C), which subsequently transforms into a protective ZrB12 intergranular phase, thereby enhancing densification, structural integrity, oxidation resistance, and liquid-metal corrosion durability relative to both conventional single-phase ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C and previous lower-temperature specimens.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 powder intended for sintering
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor, controlled addition of boron carbide into the ZrB2 starting material
generation.conditions: Sintering performed under an inert atmosphere at reduced temperatures (approximately 1700–2000 °C) with an optimized cooling protocol to promote the phase transformation
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a transient eutectic liquid during sintering that later solidifies into an intergranular ZrB12 phase, effectively bonding grains and sealing defects
generation.mechanism: Boron carbide reacts at the lower sintering temperature with ZrB2 to form a small amount of eutectic liquid that facilitates rapid densification and improved grain bonding; upon cooling, this liquid transforms into a stable, intergranular ZrB12 phase that protects grain boundaries against oxidation and inhibits liquid plating-metal corrosion pathways
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated composite is expected to show higher density and superior mechanical strength, as well as markedly improved oxidation and corrosion resistance compared to both high-temperature sintered single-phase ZrB2 and previously reported low-temperature specimens without the additive
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (density, mechanical properties, oxidation and corrosion resistance) of conventional single-phase ZrB2 prepared at >2300 °C and lower-temperature specimens processed without boron carbide
generation.boundary: The intervention is anticipated to be effective within a processing temperature range of roughly 1700–2000 °C and under service conditions typical for high-temperature structural applications and liquid-metal environments; effects outside these ranges remain to be tested
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of boron carbide and the detailed kinetics of eutectic liquid formation and subsequent ZrB12 phase transformation require further optimization and characterization

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group of pure ZrB2 and one group of ZrB2 with a controlled addition (e.g., 5–10 wt%) of boron carbide. Sinter both groups under identical inert atmosphere conditions at a temperature range of 1700–2000 °C and apply the same cooling regime. Compare the final microstructure, phase composition, and performance properties.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis to verify the presence of the ZrB12 intergranular phase
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructural and grain-boundary characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron carbide-modified samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in densification, formation of the ZrB12 intergranular phase, oxidation resistance, and resistance to liquid-metal corrosion compared to the unmodified ZrB2 samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys have been rapidly developed in recent years due to their simple structure, excellent mechanical properties and convenient production. According to the nature and composition of the alloy, high entropy alloys can be divided into four categories: 3D-CoCrFeNi HEAs, lightweight HEAs, high entropy amorphous alloys, and refractory HEAs. Three-dimensional group HEAs are thoroughly studied and widely used because of their stable structure, simple manufacturing process and high performance–price ratio []. Lightweight high-entropy alloys have a low density and high specific strength, and are widely used in industries with strict quality control and performance requirements, such as transportation and aerospace []. High entropy amorphous alloys have a structure with disordered arrangement of metal atoms. A high entropy amorphous alloy usually has a large elemental distribution, good magnetic properties and amorphous forming ability []. The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.
